subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the noon recess I had addressed my remarks largely to the minister's observations with respect to a fuller measure of information being made available to parliament and the people with regard to international relations and world issues generally. I think there is an urgent need to build up a constructive and intelligent Canadian opinion on world affairs from one end of Canada to the other. In my opinion Canadians are hungry for a knowledge of world affairs.
As I look from one end of this chamber to the other I see a great number of hon. members who from time to time have taken it upon themselves to speak in various parts of Canada with respect to foreign relations. I think it might properly be said that many of us have spoken more on that subject than perhaps we have on any domestic issue. I think most of us who have done so have found that there is a great interest on the

part of the citizenry of this country in the problems which this parliament and government face. The Department of External Affairs ought to see to it that in the days that lie ahead the conditions which have existed in the days gone by shall not be perpetuated and that the government and the department take the people of Canada more fully into their confidence with respect to world affairs generally.
We should know what is going on outside this nation through information coming from governmental sources. We should know further what the government may decide from time to time they are going to do about it. On that score I am impelled to refer the house to the penetrating and constructive criticism of Mr. I. Norman Smith of the Ottawa Journal, an experienced observer in the field of international relations. Mr. Smith had something to say on this point only two weeks ago when he was writing from Lake Success. After taking the minister and his department to task in a friendly way for refusing to take the public of Canada into their confidence on the vital happenings in the world from day to day, and expressing the conviction that there is a great deal of news about what is going on in the world that Canadians do not get, he declared that while the Department of External Affairs gets that news and shapes its policies upon it, it only comes to the Canadian people in the form of the final decision.
One observation he made was that it is no answer to say that diplomatic information must not be let out. The British let out much more and so do the United States. Mr. Smith goes on to say:
We lack informed controversy. And Informed controversy makes for enthusiastic public support of intelligent foreign policy.
The end effect of our present policy of secrecy is that we are told virtually nothing about the situation until suddenly we are told we are breaking diplomatic relations or refusing trade or even going to war.
Mr. Smith is not a man who thus speaks out without some provocation, and were it not for my limited time today I should like to quote him more fully. What he said has been emphasized lately in this chamber when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was asked in the house just a short time ago what Canada was going to do at the United Nations when the vote came for the Czechoslovakian or Yugoslavian candidature for a non-permanent seat on the security council. The Prime Minister indicated very clearly that in his opinion the question ought not to have
External Affairs
been asked because it was the practice of the administration not to tell anybody what the government of Canada was going to do.
Not only were we not told what instructions were given on that occasion to the Canadian delegation; nobody has found out yet which way we voted. One would almost imagine that the Canadian people had no right to know what side they were being put on in New York and that the decision must remain locked up with only the government and its senior officials holding the key. We in Canada know how the United States and Britain voted, but apparently we are not to be informed of our own stand. I think we in this parliament and the people generally are entitled to that sort of information so long as the safety and security of the nation is not at stake.
Recently the United States government announced its intention to appoint a separate assistant secretary of state who would be charged with the specific responsibility of assisting the people in that nation to keep pace with the foreign policies of the government and its growing influence in world affairs. Such a move apparently seemed commendable to the United States government, not only on the ground that it helps its citizens to understand the foreign policies of the government, but for the more important reason that it recognizes that a foreign policy without public support could very easily become no foreign policy at all.
I am not suggesting that we should follow that move in all the details I have described. I think we have the machinery in our own Department of External Affairs which would make a drastic move of that kind unnecessary. There is in the Department of External Affairs an information division which in the main does a satisfactory job, but its activities must necessarily follow and not precede government decisions on policy. The result is that little information becomes available as to the various backgrounds upon which our foreign policies are based. I submit that full information is much more essential now that the government has retreated from its former policy of having multiple-party representation at the United Nations, although I am not suggesting that the government should go back to that practice at the moment.
When the government gets away from the people, whether on domestic issues or in the international field, there is always a tendency for a department to form itself into a little clique that thinks it knows better than the people the amount of information and the details thereof that should be given. We had a good example just before the house rose

External Affairs
tor the noon recess. A question arose which I think is of vast concern and interest to the people of Canada generally. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) spoke about the commonwealth of nations rather than the British commonwealth of nations. I am quite sure I have been guilty of doing so myself, and I imagine that other members on all sides of the house have also done so from time to time. For purposes of abbreviation the expression "commonwealth of nations" may sometimes be used inadvertently without the adjective "British", but I certainly think that we who have been guilty of that abbreviation from time to time would not want it understood that because we used the abbreviated form we meant something other than the British commonwealth of nations.
I want to say to the minister and the government that I think the services and contribution of Great Britain in the two world wars, which proved the bastion and bulwark of democracy, are enough to make the Canadian people proud to put the word "British" before the words "commonwealth of nations". I think no one has any need to apologize for that. I have no particular objection to people abbreviating, but I suggest that when they do so they ought to make it clear in the abbreviation that they mean the British commonwealth of nations.
It seems strange to me that an issue which is so important to the people should be casually put before parliament on an occasion such as this, and that we should learn officially for the first time in an introductory message from the minister that in some respects this country has turned its back upon the designation, "British commonwealth of nations", and has now adopted "commonwealth of nations". I think that only emphasizes what I have been trying to say, that we are not getting enough of the background and information whereby an intelligent opinion can be formed. That is a good example of the kind of surprise to which the parliament of Canada should not be subjected in this enlightened age.
I wish now to deal with the activities of the department and the minister. With the steady invasion of Canada into the field of foreign relations, accelerated greatly by our magnificent contribution, if I may say so, in two world wars, which gave us a prominent place at the San Francisco conference and has given us a prominent place in all international gatherings since that time, it is only natural that the department should have grown with great rapidity. As a matter of fact, it has grown to a high level of importance

among the units of governmental administration at Ottawa. I think it is only fair to say that the department has attached to its personnel some of the ablest public servants of whom Canada can boast, and many of them young veterans of the last world war. It is a well-known fact that in the councils of the world-and those of us who have served with some of these officials overseas and in other places can bear testimony to what I am saying-our external affairs representatives have played a leading part. I desire to pay tribute to those who have played so important a role for Canada in its relations with other countries at global gatherings.
As far as possible, in my opinion, the issue of determining peace and war should not be subject to thoughtless or synthetic criticism. Nevertheless it is the duty of the opposition, by way of stimulating suggestions and careful examination, to make sure that the new department operates efficiently. Perhaps I should not use the word "new" because it is not new except in its recent development. The Department of External Affairs has mushroomed from a personnel of 392 in 1941 to a present total of 1,248. I think it is important that the opposition and parliament make sure that, by reason of inadequate constructive criticism, we do not allow the department to be the spoiled child of either the government or parliament.
I should like to say further that I am not particularly critical of the expenditure of money on our external affairs. I think of course that the opposition must always be on the alert to see that the taxpayer gets the best value for every dollar that is spent. I merely want to point out to the minister and to the department generally that in certain respects I think we ought carefully to scrutinize their expenditures. Canada's population constitutes only one out of every 188 of the entire world's population, and has a relatively small national income compared to some of those with which we have to compete. It is hard to avoid the human weakness of trying to keep up with the international Joneses. Sometimes the international Joneses have a much deeper purse from which to draw than we have. I am not pointing to any special detail of the department except to indicate that, although Canada's foreign affairs have largely been lifted out of the realm of narrow controversy from a party point of view, at the same time we must watch that the department does not in the future-and I am not saying it has done so in the past-run wild so far as its expenditures and these other matters are concerned.

I come now to another point, and I do so without reflection upon any of our present diplomatic representatives abroad. I think it can properly be said that, as far as possible, we should have representing us at the capitals of the nations of the world Canadians who are truly representative of some of the great sections of our population. They are our show windows. More often than not Canada is judged in a foreign country by the one man who goes from this dominion to represent us at that nation's capital. I think it will be at once seen how important it is today to choose the right man for the job, because of the increased importance of our international relations generally. We should be training for our senior diplomatic posts men whose backgrounds are solidly rooted in some of the main occupations of our people. At once it will come to the minds of hon. members that the Canadian farmer, the Canadian workman, the Canadian businessman, and Canadian women are four sections of the population out of the many that could be mentioned, but I think it is time we set out to formulate a policy whereby we shall ensure that our representatives in other countries will be truly representative of the Canadian people, their occupations, their ideals and so forth.
We draw men for diplomatic posts from some of the professions, but so far as I know we have pretty well neglected the agricultural colleges of our nation when we seek material for diplomatic representation abroad. We have not gone to the trade unions for material either, and in my opinion this shows a lack of practical vision which is rather essential for our future success in the diplomatic field. Therefore, I say it is time to pause, take inventory and construct a virile practical policy in so far as our foreign representation is concerned.
Before I leave the subject of the department itself I want to suggest to the government an amendment to the legislation creating the Department of External Affairs. I fancy the minister himself may find this suggestion rather welcome, as I hope other members of the house will. We should not have to continue to go through the agony of referring to the minister as the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Worse than that, we have to refer to the under-secretary of state for external affairs, and I believe there is still the further title of associate undersecretary of state for external affairs. If for no other reason than economy in printing, my suggestion ought to meet with favour. The terminology is clumsy, cumbersome and confusing. I suggest that the head of the
External Affairs
department should be known, as he is practically always called now, as the Minister of External Affairs and his deputy as the deputy minister of external affairs. I have made this suggestion previously, but I want to press home upon the government the desirability of making this change in the interests not only of the minister and his deputy but of parliament and the people, and particularly the press.
Now for a moment I should like to deal with Canada's cardinal foreign policy. In all the speeches that are made and the discussions that take place from time to time I believe we must never lose sight of the fact that the cardinal policy for Canada must be the maintenance of permanent peace and security for our people. Around this desirable and essential objective we must range our diplomatic moves. This nation has a key part to play in peace, for no nation has a greater stake in international harmony than Canada. We have nothing to gain from war; we never did have anything to gain from war. We have everything to gain from peace. Our national objectives here at home, looking to the development of a heritage that no other people in the world have been privileged to enjoy, are predicated upon the nations of the world remaining at peace with each other. So I say, in the interests of ourselves and of others, our cardinal policy must never be lost sight of in the many diplomatic discussions that take place dealing with foreign affairs. We must never depart from the objective of international co-operation, understanding and peace.
It is easy to belittle the work of the United Nations; and I was pleased to hear what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) had to say just a few hours ago in that regard. In many quarters it is fashionable to decry the work of that organization. I believe we as a nation should refuse to join the hue and cry against a well inten-tioned, if perhaps at times rather futile, instrument for collective security and world peace. When the shortcomings of the United Nations are being carefully inventoried and told in colourful language, it is well to remember that a perfect organization for peace is impossible in a yet imperfect world. We should not lay all the blame on the doorstep of the United Nations organization. It is frequently forgotten-I do not think the minister mentioned this in his hurried review this morning, but I want to mention it now- that when the United Nations organization was formed at San Francisco it was predicated upon what the world felt was a proper assumption; that is, that before it undertook any major operations we would have peace treaties between the nations that took part

External Affairs
in the last war. Instead of that, however, the United Nations has been forced to operate on a basis which was never contemplated. Peace treaties have not been signed, except with minor countries in Europe. The major peace treaties are outstanding, and perhaps that is one of the principal reasons why there is so much confusion, despair and discouragement with respect to the work of the organization.
Some of us in this house who were present when the organization was born at San Francisco are perhaps more discouraged and disappointed than anyone else. It was natural that we should have glorious hopes with respect to what that great organization might do. But to those who are enemies of the United Nations, those who are perhaps thoughtless opponents of that organization, I say we should pause and just think back as to what kind of world this would have been if there had been no positive and organized plan for permanent peace as the last armed holocaust drew to a close. Had that happened, in effect the nations of the world would have been admitting bankruptcy in ideals and objectives, and indeed in the field of world peace itself.
I do not think I want to go as far as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) went some time ago, when he referred to one of the main organs of the United Nations as being "frozen in futility and divided by dissension", though I have no doubt that at times he must have felt that this description fitted it. I am not so sure I would go that far, however, and I do not think parliament generally wants to go that far. Nevertheless I think that as a nation we must realize that no matter how determined our country may be to preserve world peace, we cannot hope to bring about that peace, security and prosperity by our own efforts alone. Let us start with that assumption, no matter what party we may belong to in this House of Commons, because it is a stark, naked fact in this very uncertain world of today. Out of this realization was born the United Nations, a world-wide effort to organize peace-loving countries in a search for peace and progress on a universal scale. Unfortunately the effort to achieve collective security through this medium has not been as successful as had been hoped by the founders at San Francisco, because of the obstruction of a minority small to begin with but which has been increasing in numbers and power for a considerable time.
When we speak of that minority we might as well mention those to whom we refer. It is Soviet Russia and her satellite states who have been endeavouring to create chaos and confusion in the very organization that was

set up to preserve peace and harmony in the world. As a result freedom-loving nations have proceeded with a search for collective security on another broad basis, yet within the charter of the United Nations itself. Our government, with the full endorsation of the people, have followed such a foreign policy and I believe are determined to continue to follow it. That policy is set out in the North Atlantic treaty.
Therefore I want to sound a note of warning against any tendency to underestimate or undervalue the work of the United Nations. There is a very definite and important job for this organization to do through its various agencies. In some respects it is doing that job. I believe it must still be given a chance to slowly but effectively knit and weave the pattern of international unity on a universal scale. We in Canada must never flag nor fail in our resolute quest for a just and lasting peace.
Before I leave the subject of the United Nations, I should like to mention that, after the first general assembly of 1946 in London, I took occasion to warn this parliament that the United Nations might easily become a glorified debating forum if certain circumstances prevailed for any length of time. My statement was made at a time when I was calling upon President Truman, Prime Minister Attlee and Premier Stalin. I called upon them not to boycott the United Nations but to come themselves and meet on common ground annually to clear away the fog of global differences. My fear was that with secondary representatives rather than the primary chiefs in command, issues might be dodged, decisions delayed and talk might replace action. Many of my fears have proven justified. I repeat the call. If the nations of the world desire peace, then I think it is up to the chiefs of the main nations of the world to go to the United Nations. If they think it is the important body they have told the rest of the world it is, then there is some responsibility on those chiefs to go to that organization, put their feet under a table and solve some of the problems the common people of the world want them to solve.
I should like to deal with a subject which was stressed by the minister when he made his speech, but I wish to deal with an aspect of it which he did not discuss. When the international atomic energy commission was set up at the first meeting of the general assembly of the United Nations in 1946, we were pleased to see the signal role of Canada recognized. She was appointed as one of the permanent members of that commission. The

strong and constant pressure exerted by Canadian representatives from time to time down to the present crisis, urging effective international control and inspection, has in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, carried the unanimous approval of the Canadian people. It would be a tragedy of the first magnitude, I submit, if such a destructive force as the atom should be allowed to run wild in time of war. Our very civilization may well be at stake in the issues now up for decision. I cannot emphasize too strongly the argument put forward by the minister on that point this morning when he spoke of atomic energy for peaceful use-yes; atomic energy for war-no. That is the Canadian policy in a nutshell. We must proceed to try to find agreement to control the use of atomic energy.
Evidence was given before the House of Commons committee on atomic energy which points up another issue which may well involve our external relations with the great republic to the south of us. Everyone who has spoken on behalf of this government has said that, so far as Canada is concerned, our part in the development of atomic energy is the development of it for peaceful purposes and industrial use. That is what we should be doing; that is our job and the government says that is our policy.
The chairman of the Canadian atomic energy control board, in giving testimony before the committee the other day, stated that a United States law passed in 1946 prohibits Canada having with that country the same close contact she has with the United Kingdom. In a press dispatch reporting the proceedings of the committee the chairman is quoted as follows:
Internally Chalk River's heavy water radioactive pile lets Canada do research that can't be done elsewhere, that eight universities on their own initiative are doing research of large value with state aid on capital outlays, and that it is "a tragedy"-
These are the chairman's own words:
-it is "a tragedy" that secrecy requirements nre-vent industry from playing the role it could play in the atom's early era.
Since this appears to enter into the field of our external relations with the United States, we should be told what agreement or understanding on the international level these facts are predicated upon. As compared with the partnership between government and industry which characterizes the development of atomic energy on a peacetime basis in the United States, industry in Canada seems to be completely hobbled. More than that, it is said that fifty per cent of the United States atomic energy commission spending goes directly into industry
External Affairs
and appears to indicate that the United States policy, in vivid contrast to ours, is to make available to industry such information as is possible within the limits of national safety and security. This enables industry to acquire the know-how of atomic energy and its direct application to industrial uses. No doubt the significance of that will come to the mind of every member of the house.
No one doubts the immense possibilities of this form of power in the domain of medicine, biology, agriculture and industry. Its future use may usher in an era of change of as vital importance to the people of this country and the world as did steam and electricity in the days long past. Its future use may be revolutionary in character and it may open up an era of which we have never even dreamed. Yet, the head of our atomic energy control board in Canada says it is a tragedy that industry is not participating in atomic research. The reason given is secrecy.
This policy adopted by one nation and not another might easily put Canadian industry and labour behind the "eight ball", to use a street term, in the competitive field of power and other atomic uses in the future. The people should be told whether this difference in policy in Canada is a domestic governmental decision or whether it is founded on some arrangement between the two countries on the international level. If it is the latter then this house should know what that understanding or agreement is.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to another matter which is of paramount importance in the discussion of our foreign affairs today. When the Canadian signature was placed upon the North Atlantic treaty, it marked a major departure from Canada's previously expounded anti-commitment policy in the field of world relations. It meant that this nation had caught the spirit of reality in the realm of collective security and was prepared to say what this country would do in a given set of circumstances. So determined are our people that the world's war dogs shall be kept behind doors barred and locked forever, the treaty passed parliament without a dissenting vote and was endorsed by the people generally. The scant disapproval given to it was given by those who have the mistaken idea that the communist system of government is better than our own democracy. As an instrument for peace rather than an instrument for war, as an instrument within rather than without the framework of the United Nations, it became necessary when the veto-ridden security council became nearly impotent as an enforcement body. The security council

External Affairs
lacked teeth. This was to provide the teeth required to see that peace is kept on an international scale. On September 19, 1947, Prime Minister St. Laurent, speaking as Canadian secretary of state for external affairs, told the general assembly of the United Nations meeting at that time:
. . . that the nations, if forced, may seek greater safety in an association of democratic and peace-loving states, willing to accept more specific international obligations in return for a greater measure of national security.
On October 25, 1948, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), in a speech before the United Nations association in Toronto, announced that Canada's defence program was planned after consultation with others, so that what Canada might do in the way of defence would fit into any subsequent plan that might be arrived at after parliament had given approval to the Atlantic pact.
On November 26, 1948, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), in a press conference at The Hague, is reported to have said:
. . . that Canada will commit herself freely to military measures specific enough for security.
Since these statements of Canadian foreign policy were announced, Canada and eleven other countries have signed the Atlantic pact. Although the Atlantic pact was ratified at the last session of parliament, the specific obligations of that pact have not yet been made public. I am convinced that the time has come for parliament and the country to be given more facts as to our obligations under the Atlantic pact.
I read the report of the debate on Friday, in which the Minister of National Defence had something to say with respect to Canada's defence policy. If any reading of his words bears out what his intentions were, then it would seem to me that it was delightfully vague with respect to the relationship of Canada's specific commitments under the North Atlantic treaty and Canada's defence plan and policy at home. It was a delightfully vague disposal of the whole problem. More than that, I listened this morning to the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaking in excellent language, conveying his thoughts to the house in an eloquent way, but still not getting to the point as to just what were our commitments of a specific character in the way of national defence as related to the North Atlantic treaty. I suggest that the Secretary of State for External Affairs can hardly say that he is not yet ready to divulge such information, in view of his statement in the House of

Commons on September 16 last. In reply to a question he said:
The report has been considered by the government, and we think it provides a suitable basis for the organization required under the Atlantic pact, so that it can become an effective instrument for the carrying out of its primary purpose, that of assisting the United Nations in preserving peace and preventing aggression.
After all, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs can, in effect, announce to the nation on September 16 that the Atlantic defence structure, as drafted, is satisfactory to Canada, surely at this date, many weeks later, either he or the Minister of National Defence should be able to give a much clearer, much more definite and much more constructive answer than has already been given.
The Canadian people are entitled to know what it is that we are committed to under the North Atlantic treaty. Once they know what we are committed to under that treaty, there will be no doubt as to the kind of full support the Canadian people will be prepared to give to the government. When they are going to give that support, I think they are entitled to have the government take them into their confidence in connection with it. I do not think it is proper to have too many of these things kept in the exclusive preserve of the government. There are a great many things that ought to be in the exclusive preserve of the people. I cannot think that the minister will allow this present discussion to terminate without presenting to the Canadian people what it has meant in terms of commitments and present and future plans of defence for this nation to sign the Atlantic pact. Parliament and the people gave ungrudging support to the government on the principle of the Atlantic pact. I think the government ought now to give ungrudgingly the information to which the people of Canada are entitled -always, of course, within the limits of national safety and security.
Now I come to another point and that is Canada's relations with Britain and the United States. This nation's foreign policy and her very position in international affairs are influenced very materially by Anglo-American relations. More than all others there are three great powers whose friendship with us, and with each other, has made our diplomatic path easier in the past. Upon the continuance of this relationship will be founded much of our security in the future. Britain, France and the United States, without reflecting upon any other group of nations, have been singularly close to us in geography, ideals, objectives and sentiment. In two great wars all four of those nations fought

side by side. May there never come a time when our relations with any of them suffer decline.
I was interested in a reference made this morning by the minister. It was a characteristic reference of his. He said that, in our relations with the United States, after all perhaps we should not take too much for granted-and I agree with that sentiment- and that in the case of diplomacy with the United States, just as in marriage and friendship, we should not allow those relations to be weakened by neglect.
I can readily recall the foreign secretary of Britain answering a question on the floor of the United Kingdom parliament in 1945, when someone asked him at that time-and I think it was an opposition question-whether the minister did not think it would be a good thing if Britain had more meetings with the Russians as the diplomatic relations between the countries were somewhat deteriorating. I can quite well remember Mr. Bevin standing up. I can see him to this day. I wondered what kind of answer he would give. He said something to this effect: My hon. friend must surely know that many close friendships are made very much closer the less often some of these friends see each other. I could not help repeating that story today, but I do not think it applies to a relationship which is as close and intimate as that between Canada and the United States; closeness and intimacy must always remain characteristics of our relations with our great neighbour to the south.
In view of the fact that Britain is a member nation with us in the great commonwealth family and when I say "commonwealth family , I want to say that the connotation there is the British commonwealth family, so there will be no excuse for anyone questioning me in that regard if I happen to abbreviate in the future-and that we and they enjoy the privilege and honour of the same crowned head, and in consequence of the further fact that sentiment plays such an important role in our family relations, it would seem to me that an effort should be made to bring our royal family in closer contact with the people of Canada. The year 1939 was the first time that a governing monarch of Britain or Canada ever set foot upon Canadian soil.
That always seemed to me unfortunate and particularly when the unifying results which attended Their Majesties' visit at that time were so apparent and real. In my opinion, our Canadian children should not have to leave Canada to be able to see their own King and Queen. At more frequent intervals,
External Affairs
subject to the health of Their Majesties, we should have them with us in our own land. This would constitute a first step towards the laudable objective of having an itinerant crowned head, residing for appropriate periods among his several groups of subjects. Only those who have been privileged' to travel outside our borders have seen Their Royal Highnesses, the popular and idolized Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret. In my humble opinion, the government should exert every possible effort to have Princess Margaret visit Canada next year, as has been hinted in other quarters of recent days. Her beauty, charm and youth would go far to establish firmly in the hearts of the Canadian people the love and affection in which the royal family is held in every corner of this land. We can assure the princess of a welcome, the warmth of which will be matched only by that tendered to her royal father and mother a decade before, and which will be later tendered to her illustrious sister and the Duke of Edinburgh, and last but not least bonnie Prince Charlie himself.
I want to turn for a moment, if I may, to the continent of Europe, which for a long time has seen the seeds of war planted beneath her soil. I think it can be said that the establishment of the western union, the signing of the North Atlantic treaty, which brought in the power of the new world as a factor in the stabilization of Europe, the institution of the so-called parliament of Europe and the success of the west in the Berlin impasse, all played a vital part in re-establishing the position of the western democracies in the troubled European scene.
The Berlin blockade, which has since been lifted, was a turning point in the cold war for prestige in the neurotic continent of Europe. Before the Berlin impasse occurred, the prestige of the western democratic powers had reached the lowest ebb since the second world war came to a close. The shattered continent wondered what the future had in store for it; would it be democracy or communism? The western powers seemed so far away. No matter what their will was, were they able to carry it out? And at the same time the hot breath of the nearby Russian bear was blowing down their necks.
When the allied powers made a decisive stand on the Berlin blockade and organized the world's most successful airlift, it brought democracy back into the running again so far as the continent of Europe was concerned. It turned the tide. Since that time the Russian foreign ministry has changed hands. Yugoslavia seems to have mutinied, Italy has strengthened its democratic position and
18S4

External Affairs
France shows definite signs of recovery and consequent attachment to the democratic cause. The cold war has not gone so well for Russia in Europe as she had hoped, but we shall do well not to underestimate the dangers which still are so apparent there when we hear that Malenkov, one of the top members of the politburo, said in Moscow only a few days ago that Russia had the atomic bomb; that a third world war would destroy capitalism; that the United States was plotting armed intervention in countries bordering the Soviet union, but that the Soviet union of course sought nothing except peace.
We should not be lulled into a sense of false security by honeyed phrases and sweet nothings. We should realize that the threat of Russian aggression is no less because of this apparent shift in strategy.
It is now evident to Russia that the communist policy of threats and name-calling displayed in the cold war failed to shake the democracies ox their policies. This new approach is merely a shift from cold war to cold diplomacy. This new peace-talk diplomacy of Russia is not a shift of goals but merely a shift of methods designed to lead us down the primrose path of complacency along which democracies are so vulnerable.
I should like to have time this afternoon to deal with some of the things that are reported to be happening within the Soviet-controlled part of the continent, but time is fleeting. I do want however to make reference to one thing before I leave Europe. There are important current developments on the west German diplomatic front today. The minister dealt with them as best he could in the limited time at his disposal this morning. The government should furnish such facts to parliament and to the people as can safely be given, so that public opinion can crystallize with respect to the pros and cons of the proposal to bring gradually this part of Germany into the western democratic orb. It will at once be seen that this is essential in a nation like Canada which lost so many of the flower of its manhood in two wars. Keeping that in mind one will readily see how important it is; and I emphasize this upon the government with every bit of earnestness that I have at my command. I suggest to the government that they ought to give the public sufficient facts so that public opinion may be crystallized upon this particular point, because it is a matter of major importance to this nation that we have a supporting public behind any move of that kind that may be made. A confused opinion based on sketchy and inadequate facts may be a

serious matter. The house should be told whether the newspaper reports hinting at an exchange of diplomats between Ottawa and the west German capital of Bonn have any foundation in fact. We should be told, too, whether in fact the western democracies are extending their frontiers, as the Secretary of State of the United States, Dean Acheson, said only a few days ago; whether they are extending them to the banks of the Elbe. The interest of the average Canadian in the stirringly vital movements in Europe is both keen and urgent. He knows that in this war-shattered continent may well be found the answer of peace or war in the critical days of tomorrow.
I now have a word to say with respect to the Far East. With four hundred millions of people added to the vast population previously within the orb of communism it can well be said that the danger spot for democracy is shifting to the Far East. China, a permanent member of the security council and former friend of the democracies, now has by armed revolution reversed her world allegiances. This change has far-reaching consequences for us as well as the other western powers. In a sense-I want hon. members to give some thought to this, if they will-China is today in a more inferior position as a former ally than if she had been our enemy in world war II. Today she has been abandoned to imperialistic aggression by Russian communism while Japan is occupied by democratic forces striving to restore her economy and establish a free government. Such are the puzzling situations that sometimes come to our attention in world affairs.
The Canadian ambassador is back from China. He should be called before the external affairs committee to testify upon the present conditions in that war-torn land. The hearts of Canadians are sad over the plight of China, for those of her people who have come to this country have been conscientious, honest and industrious citizens and have created a most favourable impression by their conduct among us.
Therefore, Canadians would like to know whether the new pro-Russian regime in China is likely to be more communist than Chinese or more Chinese than communist. Something may depend upon that, and we should be kept abreast of the information on that crucial point. We should know what information exists on the possibilities of further communist aggression in the strategic Far East. In short, the puzzled and confusing Chinese picture should be unveiled in the interests of a more intelligent and informed Canadian public opinion.

Coming to the close of my remarks I should like to deal now with a matter which I think is of paramount importance to this house and this country, and I refer to India. Many times it has been said with effect that the British commonwealth of nations can never be a static thing. Recent world developments have proved beyond question the soundness of that statement. For years the movement for liberation and independence was guided, fostered and promoted by Mahatma Gandhi and his devoted followers in that heavily populated land. Independence finally came, but with its birth came painful internal struggles and wide divergences of opinion between followers of different religious beliefs. But out of it came Pakistan and India, out of it came a great Indian leader and prime minister.
Pandit Nehru, the many-times-imprisoned disciple of Gandhi, assumed an even more important place in the sun with the assassination of the great Gandhi himself. In the confused and puzzled picture of the Far East, Nehru stands out as the beacon light of democracy against totalitarianism. His role is a difficult one to play in the internal and international field. With China temporarily mastered by communist forces, with many obstacles to reforms existing within the Indian nation itself, Nehru's task is a herculean one. I could not help thinking as he stood in this chamber a few short weeks ago, charged with the responsibility of governing over three hundred millions of people, that for both India and Canada a new era was breaking and that a new dawn had come in commonwealth change and development. Here was a man who had spent thirteen of his most productive years in British jails. It is a testimony to his tolerance, his greatness and his common sense that, despite all that he has gone through, he prefers to leave his nation, though a republic, still within the family of the British commonwealth. It is a tribute to the United Kingdom, it is a tribute to Nehru, it is a tribute to India, it is a tribute to the British commonwealth of nations.
As he was addressing us the thought must have occurred time after time to his listeners that there stood a great commonwealth statesman upon whose shoulders was being laid perhaps the main burden of defending the Far East and its teeming millions from the invasion of atheistic communism. Nehru's visit to Canada was more than an accident; it was a symbol of a coming understanding between east and west. It provided an opportunity for closer relationship between this great dominion and India as well as her sister dominions of Pakistan and Ceylon. In the light of all this I should like at this time
External Affairs
to make what I hope will be a constructive and far-reaching suggestion. I know it will be breaking new ground.
If the Prime Minister of Canada has not already received an invitation from the Indian government to pay a visit to India, and I rather fancy he has, then I think it should be made known to the Indian government and its Prime Minister that the Canadian Prime Minister would welcome an invitation to visit India at a convenient time, some time after the close of the next session of this parliament, and that he should institute for the first time in diplomatic history and provide personal leadership to a goodwill trek of representative Canadians to the new Indian nation and to our other commonwealth sisters in the east.
In the years that lie ahead, many Canadians will be going to India and other Far Eastern areas for business, diplomatic and other reasons. Such a good will visit by our own Prime Minister and by leading representative people from both our urban and our rural Canada, not confined to diplomats, not confined to men in politics, not confined to men in business, but broadly speaking a small but significant cross-section of the Canadian people, would be heralded the world over as a visit which broke new ground in a new era of international good will, co-operation and understanding. It would show the Indian people that Canada is interested in them, that Canada wants to be a co-operative sister with her in the great British commonwealth family, and that Canada is anxious that we shall establish as soon as possible a good trading relationship, because very often friendship flows with trade. And when that good will party, led by the Prime Minister, comes back to Canada, its very representative personnel would be able to take into the corners of Canada the story of India and her possibilities and the homes of Canada would be made more familiar with India, her problems, her people and her possibilities. This nation should not let this opportunity pass. We should be the first to extend a personal word of greeting through our own Canadian folk to the Indian people at large. It would be the major move in uniting east and west in a closer and more co-operative British commonwealth family.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that my first word in taking part in this debate can be one of congratulation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on the thoughtful and comprehensive review of Canadian external relations which he has

External Affairs
given to this house. I hope it will not prove an embarrassment to the minister if I say that the members of the C.C.F. liked his speech, not only because of the way in which it was delivered and the information it supplied but more so because of the moral and social philosophy which we felt was so much a part of it. I am sure the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) will pardon me if I do not follow him in the very forceful speech he made, but I do want to touch on one point which he raised at the beginning of his speech. It may not be an important point, but I think it is desirable that it should be settled and I think it is one of those points in our foreign relations that can be settled.
The hon. member objected to the term "commonwealth of nations," and maintained it should be "British commonwealth of nations." I had the feeling that that term was settled upon when the prime ministers met in London last April. I understood that it was not really a matter of choice, it was a question of whether there would be a British commonwealth of nations with two or more of the most important nations outside of it just because of its name, or whether we should have a commonwealth of nations in which the countries of India and Pakistan would be partners. That was my understanding and I notice that in British literature the term "commonwealth of nations'' is used and not "British commonwealth of nations." As far as I am concerned the name is not important; what is important is the spirit of commonwealth. I am sure it will be there regardless of what name may be used.
I take part in the debate today with great hesitation. My hesitation is not because I have not arrived at conclusions about many of the problems discussed today. It arises from the fact that the issues involved in our international affairs are so varied and complex that the layman with his limited knowledge is not always sure if the conclusions arrived at are the right ones.
This afternoon I shall deal with a phase of our relations with other countries which I believe to be of paramount importance, and about which I have some understanding. I have in mind our economic relations. I am aware that economics and politics, nationally and internationally, are closely related. I am convinced that if the economic relations of the nations of the world do not run smoothly it is most unlikely that political relations will be satisfactory. I am also convinced that good economic relations
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
among the nations of the world are necessary if we are to have progress, prosperity and peace.
Like the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and indeed, all parties in the house, I accept the United Nations as the basis for our external relations. Nevertheless Canada's external affairs involve a great deal more than the United Nations because what can be done in that body is limited. Even if there were not the opposition of the Soviet union, I think that the limits imposed by the unwieldly character of the organization would make it impossible for the nations of the world to carry on all their efforts through that body.
We know that the United Nations is a divided institution. It is not divided into a government and an opposition as this house is, but is divided into a majority and an opposition. May I say that Andrei Vishinsky is the opposition leader par excellence to anyone who wants to take lessons in what a leader of an opposition should be. He knows exactly what he is going to say in every debate before he leaves Moscow for Lake Success. Every debate is a violent accusation of the motives and intentions of the other members, and at the end of it he will always say no.
It was my good fortune to attend the second session of the United Nations assembly in 1947 as one of the parliamentary advisers to the Canadian delegation. In the six weeks that I had the opportunity of watching the proceedings of the assembly or its committees, never once did Mr. Vishinsky say that he agreed with anything that was proposed unless it was proposed by the Soviet bloc. That is what makes one almost despair of the United Nations. Indeed, I felt most pessimistic about its value during the time I spent there. I think the farther one is away from it the more hopeful one is that it may be of some use in settling world problems. That does not mean, however, that the Soviet union may not change its mind some day.
I have mentioned Mr. Vishinsky. I should also like to say that I am indeed pleased to note that the Canadian delegation to the United Nations assembly has begun to talk to Mr. Vishinsky in the only language that he understands. They are talking back to him. When I was there in 1947 I thought the only delegate who talked back to Mr. Vishinsky was Hector McNeil of Great Britain. I am glad indeed to see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and only yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made speeches in which they talked to Mr. Vishinsky in the only terms that he understands.

I have had long experience in debating with communists, and I learned early that the only way to reply to them when they become belligerent is to become more belligerent.

speechtext:
The way I talk to anyone who starts to get nasty. I likened the United Nations organization to a parliament, but of course there is a vital difference. In a parliament when the opposition has done its best or its worst, whichever way you look at it and I imagine the way you look at it depends on what side of the house you are on, the majority settles the question, and that finishes it. In the United Nations the minority makes the decisions, and the minority in this instance decides that nothing shall be done about things that matter. That is the real result of the veto in the security council.
I come now to the next point I wish to make. If we cannot do through the United Nations everything that we would like to do about our international affairs, then we must decide to do these things in other ways. We have already adopted that procedure. Less than a year ago the countries on both sides of the Atlantic ocean decided to enter into a treaty for collective defence. I was glad that the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to that treaty today, and that he referred to a phase of it in regard to which I am to say a few words. I am firmly convinced that, while the treaty provides for economic as well as military co-operation, we have not done as much to promote and co-ordinate economic co-operation amongst the nations signatory to the Atlantic pact as we have on the military side. The minister referred to article 2 this forenoon, but he did not read it. I think I will read it so hon. members may see that it is quite explicit with respect to the matter of economic co-operation:
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and wellbeing. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
I agree that there has been some cooperation; but in my opinion the efforts at co-operation in the economic field have been half-hearted and not very successful. That is all-important, in my view, because if the nations of the North Atlantic pact are not economically strong they cannot be militarily strong, because our military strength will depend upon our economic strength. So it seems to me, and I have been thinking about
External Affairs
this for some considerable time, that the most disturbing aspect of our external relations, apart from the refusal of the soviet bloc to co-operate with other countries in the United Nations, is the fact that the western nations themselves do not accept co-operation as being good in itself. What has been done through Marshall aid was not done so much to help the countries of Europe build up their economies and improve their standards of living because that was desirable in itself. It was done more as a means of fighting communism, which at the time was becoming a threat to the peace, and not only the peace but the political stability, of several of the countries of Europe.
Yet co-operation has justified itself in times so recent as to be still within the memory of all. I refer, of course, to the cooperation among the countries opposed to Germany and Japan in the last war. So I would urge this government and its representatives to stress to other countries, and to practise as its own policy, economic co-operation with all the countries of the world who are willing to co-operate with us. In my opinion economic co-operation is absolutely essential if we are to lay the foundation for an enduring peace. I agree that where possible co-operation should be carried on within the United Nations, but where that is not possible it must be carried on outside that organization. We must always remember that when economic relations between nations are one-sided and unstable it is impossible for them to maintain mutual confidence and co-operation in other phases of their economic relationships, no matter how great or important may be those other phases of mutual interest.
In the present economic crisis of the free nations, any attempts to justify a given form of settlement largely upon the grounds of overriding political and military expediency are, therefore, in my opinion, based upon a fallacy. Unless economic settlements are both equitable and workable, the political and military efforts will be rendered not only impotent in themselves but will become provocative of friction. It is in the field of trade and commercial relationships that we encounter our greatest difficulties in this regard. I do not believe that cutthroat competition or indeed any other competition and co-operation can be carried on at one and the same time. I feel that the old concept of economic competition is impossible in the new world situation confronting us. In our economic dealings with other countries we shall have to keep in mind their welfare as well as our own. Any dealings not based upon that principle will not get us very far.

External Affairs
Today almost everyone believes that cooperation is good; that is, they believe in it in the abstract, or that it is good for the other fellow. A good example of that attitude appears in the conditions proposed by the United States when Marshall aid was first suggested to the countries of Europe. While believing in free enterprise itself, the United States virtually compelled the European nations to plan their economies, or in other words to co-operate in their economic activities. I want to make it clear that I am not finding fault with the United States for making planning and co-operation a condition of receiving aid. It was essential that this be done. The idea I wish to convey is that international planning and co-operation cannot stop with the countries of Europe. It must also include, at least among the Atlantic pact countries, the United States and Canada.
In his speeches both here and in Europe Paul G. Hoffman, economic administrator, never wearies of insisting that the people of Europe plan and co-operate. I do not know whether he realizes that planning and co-operation will not produce the results desired, that is progress and stability in Europe, if the largest and strongest nation in the western group does not participate fully in that co-operative effort. Mr. Hoffman spoke to the Canadian chamber of commerce in Montreal on October 27. His speech was reported in the Montreal Gazette of the following morning, and I should like to read a few words from that report because I believe they support the point I am trying to stress. Speaking of the attitude of the American people toward foreign aid and European affairs he said there was "sleepiness, apathy and wishful thinking" on the part of the people. Then he continued:
One would suppose that after two world wars and the threat of another, there would be little apathy about what was going on in the community of our neighbours. How much does it take to make us realize that we are living in an inescapably interdependent world? ' How long will it be before we understand that if we, the free nations of the world, want to avoid world war III we must stick together and work together?
It is not that we must fight together, but we must work together if we are going to avoid another world war. That, Mr. Speaker, is the point I wish to make in this debate, that we must work together for the good of each other and not each one for himself. That is as true of nations as it is of individuals.
Mr. Hoffman is only one of a great many prominent men who have recently made statements stressing the urgent necessity for economic co-operation among the nations if we are to get through this crisis, and if we

are to eliminate poverty and put our economic order on a stable basis. All these men do not use the same words, but they did stress the interdependence of the nations of the world and the necessity of co-operation.
As my next witness in this case, I should like to bring Canada's Minister of Finance. I am sure that members opposite and the members on my far right will be glad to listen to what the Minister of Finance has to say. I am reading from the "External Affairs Bulletin" for October, which contains a report of the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) at the sterling-dollar meeting in Washington at which representatives of Qanada, the United States and Great Britain were present.
Referring to the origins of the crisis the Minister of Finance said:
As to their origins, we know that they are found, largely, in the upheaval on the various countries that took part in them. We don't forget that from 1939 to 1945 the people of the United Kingdom- whose present financial difficulties' bring us here- were mobilized for total war to' an extent not reached by the other western allies; and that the gigantic effort then made is a major source of the difficulties which they are experiencing today. We also know that when victory was won they did not relax. They kept on working. We in Canada pay tribute to that spirit-and to the magnificent assistance and encouragement given to it by the government and people of the United States.
The two things together make a fine chapter in the story of co-operation between countries. It would be nothing less than tragedy-from which only the men behind the Kremlin walls would benefit-if that co-operation in which Canada and I'm sure other countries would wish to share-could not be effectively continued in the search for a solution to the problems on our agenda. Certainly no solution can be found except through co-operative action-
One can see how often the word "co-operation" comes into the statement.
Certainly no solution can be found except through co-operative action-extending beyond this meeting. Such action means, of course, more than finding a solution which requires action only by someone else.
In recent months the western democracies have made great progress in building a structure for political co-operation, particularly through the Atlantic pact. In that pact, we recognize the simple but essential fact that an attack on one is an attack on all and that we will, individually and in concert, take the necessary action to restore and maintain security. That principle is as important in economic as it is in political co-operation. In fact, one may not be able to exist without the other. Economically and in the field of human welfare our fortunes are also linked and we go up or down together.
I should like to repeat the last three lines.
That principle is as important in economic as it is in political co-operation. In fact, one may not be able to exist without the other. Economically and in the field of human welfare our fortunes are also linked and we go up or down together.
I do not believe that anything could make the urgent necessity of economic co-operation as well as military co-operation more clear

than the words of the Minister of Finance. If there is not military aggression, the one will not be needed; but whether or not there is military aggression the prosperity not only of Canada but of the European countries- indeed of the countries of the whole world- depends upon co-operation amongst the nations.
Referring to another of the world's prominent people, I may say that Dean Acheson, the Secretary of State of the United States, spoke along similar lines at a meeting of the national foreign trade council about two weeks ago. He pointed out to the people of the United States-I should like the members to note this-that gifts of goods and money to other countries was not enough. He said there must be co-operation in trade. The United States must buy as well as sell if there is to be a balance in world trade and stability in economic affairs. May I say that here-in the matter of trade-is where the great difficulty arises because so many countries today are organized to produce the same things, to build the same things, or to provide the same services.
I am convinced that if we are to have any freedom of trade, it must mean more than the removal of trade barriers. We shall have to sit down with the countries of the world and decide what we are prepared to take from them in the way of goods and services, and what they are prepared to take from us. It will be poor economy, indeed useless, for us to be competing as to which one can more cheaply produce the same type of goods or, indeed, come to the point where goods are being subsidized in order that they may be sold abroad.
It would be quite easy, Mr. Speaker, to multiply many times the few names I have mentioned of men prominent in different phases of world affairs who are convinced that economic progress, if not the survival of civilization itself as we know it depends upon closer co-operation among the nations of the world than we have had up to now. That co-operation, let me repeat, must first be in economic matters. Political co-operation cannot long survive competition or a policy of everyone for himself. I stress this point now because it seems to me that we are approaching a new phase in international relations. The war co-operation and the pooling of resources for war purposes came to an end with the end of hostilities. Then came the phase of rebuilding the economies of the countries engaged with us in the war and of some enemy countries as well. We were also catching up on the shortages of goods and services in our own countries. I believe that stage, too, is about finished.
External Affairs
I do not mean that the damages of war have been repaired or the dislocations caused by the war overcome. We must realize that the productive capacities of the countries of Europe have now been restored to a point where, in some countries, it is greater than pre-war. As always happens under our system, it creates a struggle for markets. A struggle for markets must be resolved in co-operation. Otherwise the struggle for markets, if it does not lead the western nations themselves into war, will destroy that co-operation that has been so helpful from the beginning of the war to now.
Not only that-and this point also was mentioned by the minister in his speech- but we have to consider Germany and Japan, two former enemy countries. With the assistance of the victor nations, they too are building their economic and political institutions and have already restored them to such a point that, very shortly, Canada in concert with the other nations of like mind must, in my opinion, decide where those people are going to fit in the community of nations. Where will there be a market for the enormous production of the industrial capacity of the countries of Japan and Germany? These are questions that we must solve before we are sure of peace. Again, in my opinion they can only be solved through economic co-operation.
Some few weeks ago this parliament extended a warm and sincere welcome to Pandit Nehru, the prime minister of India. I was glad to note that the welcome he received here was repeated when he visited my city only a few days later. Perhaps no other visitor to that city has received a warmer and more spontaneous welcome than that which was given to the prime minister of India.
I should like to pause here just for a moment, because members of this house are sometimes critical of the present government of the United Kingdom. But I wonder whether we in Canada appreciate the service which the Labour government did for the democratic peoples of the whole world when they gave unconditional independence to India and Burma. Just think of what the situation would be in Asia today if that independence had been withheld or if India had gained her independence by force; surely we must all realize that the situation in Asia would be much darker today than it is. I would agree with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), although possibly not just exactly in the same terms, that the time is ripe for closer economic co-operation between India and Canada.

External Affairs
I am not pessimistic about the future. I do not say that I am optimistic either. But on balance, I believe there are in the world trends toward both economic and political co-operation. I do not think anyone could have heard the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) today without feeling that he also is thinking in that way. Any pessimism on my part arises from the fact that I fear that we are too lackadaisical about peace and war. I am afraid we have not nearly as much time as we think we have, and that we should move much faster in seeking the economic and political co-operation of other nations that think as we do. In that way only can we find a permanent solution to the difficulties of our time.
There are indications in that direction. In the Ottawa Citizen of November 11-that is Armistice day-there was a report of a conference held at Canberra, Australia, where representatives of Britain, New Zealand and Australia met to discuss "the extension of friendly relations as the best bulwark against any extremist or disruptive developments in southeast Asian countries."
The Secretary of State for External Affairs today mentioned the situation in the Far East, and he rightly said, I think, that we were interested in the east because of our Pacific coast as well as in Europe because we border on the Atlantic ocean. I wonder why we, as a member of the commonwealth, did not have a representative at Canberra. I think these meetings are just as important as any others; Canada has today just as many interests on the Pacific coast or in the Pacific ocean as it has on the Atlantic ocean.
I am just about finished, Mr. Speaker; I have only one or two words to say.
