speechtext:
I feel certain, Mr. Speaker, that the entire world situation has resolved itself into a struggle between communism and democracy. It is not enough to use the words "communism" and "democracy". Those words have been bounced around so often that they have come to mean all things to all men according to the individual using them. The words have sometimes been used deliberately to confuse and confound.
I ask the government: What do they regard as the meanings of these words? Does communism merely mean the governing of nations by men whose first loyalty is to Stalin? Does democracy merely mean the government of free nations, so-called, with free parliaments, so-called? To me the meaning is much deeper. When one once gets the deeper meaning, the struggle is seen in its true light and appears to be more intricately involved and more intense.
Right here I do not think I could do better than to quote from an article which appeared not long ago in Redbook magazine. This was written by J. Edgar Hoover, director of the federal bureau of investigation in the United States. In his article Mr. Hoover pulls no punches. No one will doubt that when Mr. Hoover writes an article for publication he means what he says. I quote:
The struggle between communism and democracy is more than a clash of political ideologies. It is the offensive of atheism against all forms of religions that base themselves on the belief in God.
Until we get that, we shall never be able to diagnose properly the extent of the disease which is beginning to grip the world. Perhaps it may appear that I am reverting to the practice of my profession when I speak in these terms; but may I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that at the opening of each session of this house it is your privilege to read a prayer which I believe is one of the greatest ever penned. I have tried in my small way to find out who penned that prayer and I have not been successful. In that prayer, unceasingly day by day, you pray on behalf of this house, "Thy kingdom come". Perhaps I might be so bold as to take you back to Holy Writ and show you where one of the greatest prophets of all time declared to the house of Israel: Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government shall be upon his shoulder.
Seen in that light, the struggle I believe, becomes one between satanic powers and God's righteous power. Fundamentally it is a struggle in this world between Satan on the one hand and Christ on the other, each having a program. The satanic program is for the

External Affairs
eventual setting up of a ruthless world dictatorship while the other program is designed to establish eventually the kingdom of God on earth. The spoils of battle are the very souls, the very bodies, the very hearts and minds of the human race.
What all men in public life must determine, yea what the government above everyone else must determine, is whether this or that movement fits into the one program or the other. When it comes to government policy we must ask: Does this aid and abet the program for the eventual realization of a world satanic dictatorship, or does it aid in exposing the enemies of men, and assist in the program for the eventual establishment of the kingdom of God on earth when government shall be upon his shoulder?
Perhaps right here I should read a further extract from the article by Mr. J. Edgar Hoover. I want hon. members to notice this, because not only members of the government but every individual in public life, whether he be a government official, whether he be a teacher, whether he be a clergyman, or whatever he is, has reason to take note of these words. Mr. Hoover says:
To every honest student of communism, the evidence is clear and unequivocal that communism is anti-God, anti-Christ and anti-moral. Communism is religion's mortal foe. . .
No religion, denomination or sect has been spared the fury and contempt of the communists. God is their foe, and God's power over the civilized world is a barrier to their advances. The communist printing presses turned out thousands upon thousands of posters portraying God, Christ and religion in the vilest and most obscene manner conceivable.
The article goes on to bring out a point which I think should be impressed upon all public men and those who are interested in world affairs, and I quote:
Many communist fronts have operated under the guise of some church commission or religious body. It is ghastly to see the monster atheism being nourished in the churches which it seeks to destroy. Church leaders can stop this nefarious infiltration by taking vigorous action in the boards and commissions under church supervision. Individual ministers and church members can avoid being hoodwinked if they will stay close to the fundamentals of their faith. Any minister who cannot find in his Bible sufficient argument for the cause of liberty and social justice-who has to borrow the double-talk of the communists-is in the wrong profession and should' be carefully watched by his official superiors and by his congregation.
I for one in my capacity as a clergyman will say "Amen" to J. Edgar Hoover's remarks in that respect. When we are dealing with communism, we are dealing with a satanic force, the most powerful force on earth next to the almighty power of an omnipotent God. The struggle is one for world conquest. High ranking communists
[Mr. Hansell.i
regard no price as too high, no sacrifice too great, as long as they can gain the ends of their satanic attempts to frustrate and defeat the purposes of God for the full and complete redemption of mankind, and the establishment of the kingdom of God on earth.
I have read rather considerably about the investigations that have been made in the United States by their congressional committees and subcommittees as to un-American activities. Without taking the time to read from some of their reports, I will say that these committees conclude that the intellectual doctrine of communism has frozen and does not change. Let us remember that in all our dealings with this vicious force. The forces of communism in their essential principles and objectives never change. Tactics may, strategy may, but their objectives never change. When we think of communist forces in that respect our minds turn to the way in which they deal with political offenders. I am not going into all the details, but one cannot help believing that these communist forces are satanic when one reads of the recent trial of Cardinal Mindszenty. His trial was one of the most inhuman and ghastly pieces of work that have ever been perpetrated upon any human being. The amazing and ghastly thing is that it was done according to satanic and communist concepts in the name of justice.
Is the danger over in Canada? We have not heard a great deal about these forces since the spy trials of a few years ago. I trust that those responsible for law and order in Canada are not resting upon their oars on the assumption that, since they were able to round up a few spies and send one or two of them to the penitentiary, therefore all is well. In the United States recently several top-ranking communists were declared guilty of attempting by force to overthrow the government. I am afraid there may be a danger that even the people of the 'United States will sit back now that all the fanfare is over, rest upon their oars and say: Now we can rest easy. That is not the case because, if communism is as satanic as I believe it to be, they will not relinquish their efforts until they have eventually gained their ultimate objective. As the saying goes, eternal vigilance is the price of freedom.
I turn now to another phase of the subject. I do not know how to view the recent reports that the United States of America is beginning to look upon Yugoslavia with some degree of favour. I am well aware, as we all are, that Tito and Stalin have had perhaps unpleasant words. Possibly matters have

reached a rather intense state between them. In his speech this morning the minister indicated as much, but even though that may be so, I wonder if the communist regime as such in Yugoslavia is any different to what it was in the days of Mihailovich. I for one would not presume to be qualified to say whether or not the United States should give aid to Yugoslavia, but we know that negotiations have been going on which indicate that the United States looks with some favour upon supplying war potential to Yugoslavia. I understand Yugoslavia has already applied to the world bank for a loan, in order to secure enough dollars under the world monetary fund. [DOT] I am not expressing an opinion now whether the United States is doing right or wrong. I must confess my inability to arrive at a proper conclusion. I wish to say, however, that whatever is done about the relationship of the United States with Yugoslavia, I am afraid that our close connection with the United States will mean that we may automatically follow suit. I say I am not qualified to decide whether it would be right or wrong, but if we do so we must do so convinced in our own minds that communism in its essential characteristics does not change, whether it be in one of the satellite states, whether it be in Russia, or whether it be infiltrating into any other nation in the world.
I now come to China. I do not know how to view the situation with respect to our possible relationship with China. The minister gave a rather extended explanation of the situation there, and I think it was a truthful appraisal. Somehow or other I cannot free my mind from its rather confused and puzzled condition concerning our relationship with China over the past few years. Not many years ago the members of this house welcomed Madame Chiang Kai-shek to Canada. We remember her standing at the Clerk's table with microphones in front of her. We welcomed her with open arms. I happened to take some motion pictures as she was entering the parliament buildings with the former prime minister, a former speaker, the Speaker of the Senate and other dignitaries who welcomed her to the parliament of Canada. I cannot help thinking of the glorious reception given to her then. When she went to the United States a great reception was also held for her by the United States government and the people of that country. A few years later the same Madame Chiang Kai-shek came back. She did not visit Canada on that occasion but visited the United States seeking aid for her 45781-118
External Affairs
husband's regime, and what happened? The United States turned its back upon her, and sent her home.
Well, we can say what we like about the ruthlessness of the Chiang Kai-shek regime. Granting that it was ruthless in many aspects of its administration, I only ask this: was it any more ruthless when Madame Chiang Kai-shek visited North America first than when she made her second visit? Just here 1 should like to quote a passage from an article I read the other day by George Moorad, who wrote "Chiang Kai-shek: A Patriot Departs." I am going to read only one short paragraph:
As for the charges of corruption in his government-
Referring to Chiang Kai-shek.
notably not against the person of Chiang Kai-shek but rather "the men around him"-a distinction between east and west must be made. Graft is the curse of Asiatic society, but if Stalin has been unable to shoot it out of soviet Russia, it is quite unreasonable to expect the weak Chinese to hold off invaders with one hand and clean up their Augean stables with the other. In view of his uphill struggle for Chinese independence it can hardly be argued that Chiang sought profit for himself or wilfully allowed corruption to thrive around him.
And later in this condensed article:
As for America, whether we approved of Chiang Kai-shek or not, we did not hedge our bets with any other policy. Our chips were laid entirely on Chiang, and as he departs so goes our hard-won stake in China.
I have noticed in the press recently considerable space devoted to recognition of the new communist government in China. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made only passing reference to this point in his remarks. Somehow or other it seems that pressure is being brought to bear upon the nations in order to have them recognize the new government in China; but I cannot help noticing that in these press dispatches there are singular references to the various financial interests that some of the western democracies have in China. Here is one reference in an Associated Press dispatch of November 14:
Hong Kong island was ceded to Britain in 1841, and she has a lease on the Kowloon peninsula until 1997. Until then, Britain's strained economy demands an effort to keep it, recognizing the reds could hardly make it harder to hang on, and might make it easier.
Another Associated Press dispatch from Washington under date of November 12 has this to say:
Several motives are said by diplomatic authorities here to underlie the British decision to establish relations with the communists.
Britain has extensive commercial interests in China . . .

External Affairs
Then further on:
There is some internal economic pressure upon Washington to recognize Peiping, but it is relatively small. Export-import firms and shipping lines in Pacific coast ports are urging recognition for business reasons,
I repeat that I do not feel qualified to say when Canada should agree to recognize the new government in China; but after reading these dispatches suggesting that China should be recognized because of certain financial stakes in that country, can it be that recognition of the Chinese government is to be speeded up by reason of economic investments and financial considerations? Let us pause and examine any contemplated recognition of the communist regime in China or anywhere else, as far as that goes, lest we sell our principles on the auction block of financial self-interest.
With respect to the recognition of China, I spoke to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who is the leader of our national Social Credit party. I consulted him with regard to what formula we might propose for the recognition of new governments, and we came to this conclusion. The Social Credit movement favours diplomatic recognition of any country which has demonstrated (1) that it has a reasonably stable government; (2) that it has at least fairly well defined boundaries; (3) that it is independent of domination by any other country or force outside its own borders. Those are the three prerequisites we would require for recognition of any new government. My own view is that I would add another. I would say that should there be any shift of government following civil war, the new government should be given probation for a definite period of time, during which it must prove itself to be democratic in all essential principles, and its people free as we count men free.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that any diplomatic moves by our government or any other democratic government must be made with the greatest care. At the same time we must have vision and courage, and more than anything else the keenest sense of our responsibility toward the Creator of all men, our God, Who controls the destinies of worlds and nations and men, and Whose purpose is the establishment of a righteous peace among all men. Never was there a time when men talked so much of peace as they do today. And yet, never was there a time when men's hearts failed them so for fear of those things which are coming upon the earth. I plead with the government to move with the greatest caution in all that they do, particularly in the administration of their foreign policy. They should seek to determine a course that

will coincide with the purpose of God in the realization of His kingdom which we, at the commencement of every sitting of this house, pray shall come upon the earth.
If Canada does this, I am sure we can leave the rest to an all-wise omnipotent God whose purpose is the establishment of the righteous reign of His own Son when the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, when He shall reign forever and ever.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to publicly apologize to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) for interrupting him in the course of his eloquent address today.
I have already told him personally but I felt that the house was a little shocked by my interruption, and I am sorry it occurred. I was following the interesting remarks of the secretary of state so intently when he was discussing the position in regard to China and describing some of the conditions that Canada should have in mind in granting recognition to any government, that when he mentioned the "approval of the people of the country" the whole situation in Europe immediately surged to my mind. I felt like asking him in what country that is dominated by communism today have the people ever had an opportunity of expressing their opinion of the government that now dominates them.
If we are to begin with Russia and the countries that are described as satellites, in which minority communist organizations have controlled the major portion of the country, I do not think we can honestly find one country that could truly call itself democratic.

speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend has referred to Czechoslovakia. With that country in mind I went to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I told him that when I was listening to him I thought there was no country except Czechoslovakia which had accepted the communist government. The election in that country was rigged. I was under the impression, mistakenly, that Czechoslovakia had voted freely for the communist government. There are some who seem to be of a different opinion. I did not know anything about the elections being rigged, but there may be greater authorities on that subject than I am. There is no doubt about the other countries however, and there is no doubt that if the people of Czechoslovakia, after a year

and a half of the tyranny of the communists, had it to do over again they would not vote for the communist government.
I suppose most of the members in this house have been interested in this great Russian experiment in communism. I was glad to hear the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the member who just took his seat express sentiments that were certainly not in sympathy with communism. Although it is my feeling that socialism in all countries is likely to lead to communism eventually, there are many sincere socialists who detest communism. We have only to look at the experience in England to see how the British government ejected from the ranks of the Labour party those who had come out strongly in favour of communism.
I should like to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the lucid statement he gave this morning. I am sure everyone thoroughly enjoyed such a clear statement of policy on behalf of our government. As the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) has said, it is a pity we do not more frequently receive information on these important matters. It was only the evening before last that I made reference to this subject when I said we would not think there was such a country as Russia in the world, nor would we think that China was now being overrun by a horde of armies which are supported by the government of Russia. I was glad, therefore, to have the opportunity of listening to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to get his views on matters of such importance.
I believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs deserve congratulations on the manner in which they have carried on their duties at Lake Success. From what we read in the newspapers, there can be no doubt that they are up against hard-headed men who have a definite brief that they must take a certain line from which they cannot depart. This debate today affords us an opportunity of expressing our views on these important international questions. What seems to me to be most important of all is our attitude towards communism.
I believe, sir, that the mistake was made back in the days of Yalta. It probably does not do very much good to criticize two great public men such as the late President of the United States and the former Prime Minister of England. There can be no doubt about it, however, the initial mistake was made
45781-118i
External Affairs
when Poland was sacrificed to Russia. In 1940 I remember reading an article by Hilaire Belloc, who was an authority on international affairs if there ever was one, and certainly on European affairs. In 1913 he predicted exactly what was going to happen in 1914. In 1940, he wrote this:
"We shall win the war if Poland is restored to its former status with an outlet to the sea."
When the great men who were leading us at the time sacrificed the Polish people and divided up the country, giving half of it to Russia, that was the beginning of the present international troubles. The two great allies were then in the strongest position they ever were, because they had supplied enormous quantities of munitions to Russia to enable her to withstand the gigantic assault of the German armies. If Russia had not had that source of supply, who would be so bold as to say they could have won the battle of Stalingrad and driven the Germans from their country? When the Polish people were urged by the Russians to rise in Warsaw and drive out the Germans, Russia would not assist the allies in sending aid. This extraordinary situation and the failure of our statesmen to make better provision for Poland have resulted in the more complicated situation that seems to be developing from time to time.
I am sure every hon. member was glad to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaking about the conditions in Europe and the improvement in the western part of Europe. Last year and this year I had the privilege of visiting Europe. Last year in France I could see the beginnings of the work being undertaken there and could notice the energy with which the people were applying themselves to solving their problems. But this year it was obvious that great improvement had been made. Last year the people were in the throes of political troubles but eventually they got a government that lasted over a year. It was an anxious time' for the people of France when they found it so difficult to get a government that commanded the confidence of the chamber of deputies. But they did get one, and the year was a great help to them.
In Italy this year the people were in good spirits and certainly were working hard to try to re-establish their country after the conquest over the communists. I have often thought-and I have so expressed myself a number of times-that we in this country do not appreciate what a terrific menace to the world communism is. If I make some extraordinary statements in regard to the social

External Affairs
structure of this country, Mr. Speaker, it is because I have seen at first hand over in Europe the fear that exists among such a large proportion of the people of what a minority might do if, through force, it got into power. We sail along on calm and pleasant seas and everything seems all right. But we know that these other countries were strong and healthy ones at one time, under the capitalist system. What happened to them to turn them into communist countries today, or at least into countries where communism has been so strong? Not all hon. members, perhaps, are aware of the situation that exists today in France, where so many of the young people have turned their backs upon religion, do not practise any religion, and are therefore the proper soil for communist doctrine; because to my mind communism seems to grow more rapidly when it is set in soil that is without religion. Therefore the hon. member who has just taken his seat was right when he was saying how important religion was as an offset to communism.
Do hon. members recall the beginning of the United Nations at San Francisco four years ago when the dispute came up about whether in their charter they were going to say anything about the Christian religion or about Almighty God, and when it was decided, out of deference to Russia again, that nothing would be said about Almighty Ged on Whom we all depend? That was an initial mistake, and the troubles that have followed have been perhaps partly due to that cause.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made reference to Newfoundland on two occasions during his speech. He said that the airport at Gander was a great acquisition; and I have no doubt that it was a great acquisition to this country. It seems to me that our negotiators of confederation did not realize how strong a bargaining factor they had in their possession when they had the Gander airport. I hope that the negotiations that the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaks about will result in benefits to the whole of Canada, and to Newfoundland especially.
The bases were another thing about which we were worried and on which we criticized those who favoured confederation, because we were afraid that the Canadian government, if they took over those bases, would allow them to fall down. We are aware of the large amount of money-the hundreds of millions, I would say-which the United States government has spent in Newfoundland in order to build up these great bases. If the Canadian government took possession,

we were doubtful whether they could maintain them on the same scale or not; and I am certainly doubtful whether this government could do so. Certainly they could not have built them on the same scale as the Americans built them. I hope, however, that there will be friendly co-operation between the two countries and that a satisfactory solution will eventually be worked out.
The hon. gentleman referred to the visits that we had here from members of the United Kingdom government and to the importance of co-operation between that government and our own. There is no doubt about that. But I am not sure whether the United Kingdom government in its internal policy-with which I suppose we have not much concern- has been following a line that would eventually lead to good international understanding. The members of the United Nations are not supposed to be concerned with the internal policies of other countries. I intended to say that one means by which a country tries to promote good will among nations is by its representation abroad and by international exhibitions. I had the privilege of attending the international exhibition at Milan in April of this year, at which there was a Canadian exhibit. It was a fine affair. Although they did not have a large exhibit, Canadians could be proud of what they had there at that time.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext: Were there any British Columbia apples there?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
There was nothing from Newfoundland there. I inquired from those in charge of the exhibition whether they had anything from Newfoundland. They said no, that when they organized the exhibition they did not have time for that. I do not think there was anything there from British Columbia either. The exhibit from Canada was principally a fur exhibit.
There is no doubt that this country is certainly dependent, to a large extent, on friendship with the United States. This friendship that has lasted so long and has been cemented so firmly by comradeship in two great wars must continue to be the foundation stone of this country's foreign policy. Reference to the international border is, I think, a good guarantee that this friendship is going to continue. We all have many reasons for wishing that this friendship would become stronger; I have many personal reasons for that wish. Many of the people of Newfoundland have gone to live in the United States. It is said that there are as many Newfoundlanders in the city of Boston as there are in the whole of Newfoundland. There are therefore strong ties between our

little country and the United States, as I am sure there are between other provinces and that country.
It seems to me that the United States has not been given as much credit as it deserves for the tremendous work it has done on behalf of international understanding and the rehabilitation of the countries of Europe. The American people deserve the thanks of all peoples, and especially those of this country, for the way in which they have paid the money for this purpose. It is out of their pockets, out of their taxes, that they have subscribed this money to help to rehabilitate Europe, and on which this country has to some extent depended. Certainly the United Kingdom, which was in such a bad way, would never have been able to weather the storm so long as this if it had not been for the great help which she received from the United States; and I am sure that we all wish that help to continue.
Now, sir, I do not profess any right to speak on Asiatic affairs, but it seems to me that Canada, as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said, ought to be just as much concerned with what is going on in the Pacific as it is with what is going on in the north Atlantic. When Russia gets control of China, as seems inevitable now, since Chiang Kai-shek has been refused aid, what is going to stop her from organizing this vast subcontinent of 400 million people in the same fashion as she has been organizing her satellite countries in Europe? When these are organized what is going to withstand the hordes of armies that can be created out of that vast population? It seems to me that we may have to fall back, strange as it may seem, upon former enemies for assistance. A famous United States professor told us in Newfoundland many years ago, before 1939, when he described what was going to happen in Europe in the second world war, that after it was over we may have to join up with Germany to fight against Russia. It may be that the forces of Japan and the Japanese people who are comparable to the Germans in Europe, resourceful people who make good soldiers, may have to be called on. We may have to utilize these forces if we wish to withstand the influence of communism in that part of the world.
As the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said this morning, this country is only a small country when compared with other countries, and when it comes to war it is numbers that count. There is no doubt that this is a very wealthy country in proportion to its population, but when it comes to war numbers count in the long run. Russia has control of such a vast potential of war material that we have
External Affairs
to get allies wherever we can find them. I have no doubt that it is certainly in the backs of the minds of the western democracies that Japan will eventually be brought to our aid.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext: Would we need a pipe line then?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Yes, we shall probably need all the pipe lines we can get. However, I am not an authority on pipe lines.
There is one other matter about which I wish to speak, namely, Spain. The name of Spain did not appear in the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs this morning. We must recognize that Spain was the first country that stood up squarely to the communist menace, and although many people of socialist sympathies are inclined to condemn Spain outright as an authoritarian or totalitarian regime, bearing in mind the traditional form of government in that country, we have to recognize that the Spanish government of General Franco preserved Spain from communism, and perhaps preserved western Europe or the western world from communism as well. It was one of the ambitions of Lenin to light the fires of revolution not only in Russia but at both ends of the continent. Spain was to be the place where communism was to take root in the western part of Europe.
As most hon. members must be aware, the chief leaders in the satellite countries today, including Tito himself, were sent to Spain to organize communism in that country. Great credit must therefore be given to General Franco. I do not think he has had the recognition that he should have had for the work that he did in preserving Spain from the domination of communism.
As I said a moment ago, if we are to defend ourselves against communism, if that seems to be inevitable, at least we want to have all the influences we can get to help protect us from communism. In that event we must look for allies and Spain is one country with which Newfoundland has had most cordial relations for four hundred or four hundred and fifty years, almost since its discovery. She has been one of our best customers, and we have had a good deal to do with her from time to time. Her people visit our country every year to purchase fish. They seem to be very industrious and patriotic people. It seems to me that the United Nations must soon take up that problem again, grant recognition to Franco and send their ambassadors and ministers back to that country.
On motion of Mr. Browne (St. John's West) the debate was adjourned.

Business of the House BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE Mr. Fournier (Hull): Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall continue this debate. I understand there is a lengthy list of speakers for tomorrow. If perchance we conclude the debate we will take up Bill No. 144, to amend the Combines Investigation Act, and probably resolution No. 24 on today's order paper in the name of the Minister of Agriculture.
